questions.prompt: What happens to the calling thread when an `async` method reaches an `await`?
options: The thread is blocked until the awaited operation completes
Control yields back to the caller, so the thread can do other work instead of waiting
A new thread is always created to run the rest of the method
The awaited operation is cancelled
questions.explanation: The `await` keyword yields control back to the caller of the async method, so the calling thread can continue doing other work rather than waiting for the operation to complete.

questions.prompt: An async method fetches a value and returns `"Sample Data"`. What should its return type be?
options: `string`
`Task`
`Task<string>`
`void`
questions.explanation: `Task<T>` is used for async methods that return a value, so `GetDataAsync()` returns `Task<string>`. Plain `Task` is for async methods that don't return a value.

source.section: How to Return Data with Async Programming

questions.prompt: Why is asynchronous programming especially helpful for server applications?
options: It handles many concurrent connections without tying up a blocked thread for each one
It makes every operation finish faster
It removes the need for a thread pool
It lets the server skip slow requests
questions.explanation: In synchronous code each task needs a dedicated thread that is blocked while it waits, which wastes resources under heavy load. Async code uses threads more efficiently, so a server can handle many concurrent connections.

questions.prompt: What does the CLR's thread pool do?
options: It creates a brand-new thread for every task and destroys it afterwards
It keeps only the main thread and runs every task on it
It runs tasks on the GPU
It keeps a collection of worker threads that are assigned to tasks and returned to the pool for reuse
questions.explanation: The thread pool is a collection of worker threads maintained by the CLR; a thread is assigned to a ready task and returns to the pool afterwards, avoiding the overhead of creating and destroying threads repeatedly.

"Work started", then "Work finished", then "Task was canceled"

questions.explanation: The method prints "Work started" and then waits on `Task.Delay(5000, ct)`. `CancelAfter(1000)` cancels the token after one second, so the delay is cancelled, "Work finished" never runs, and the caller catches `OperationCanceledException`.

questions.prompt: How do you raise the "flag" that tells a running async loop to stop?
options: Set the `CancellationToken` variable to `null`
Call `Cancel()` on the `CancellationTokenSource`; the loop checks the token, for example with `token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested()`
Call `Dispose()` on the running `Task`
Throw an exception from the calling method
questions.explanation: The flag is set by calling `Cancel()` on the `CancellationTokenSource`; the worker cooperatively checks its token with `ThrowIfCancellationRequested()` and passes it to `Task.Delay`.
